Question: Why when a crazy event the isps slowdown but when millions watch the superbowl the cable stream isn't effected?
original:
Hey Sam,

Great question. The short version: the Super Bowl does slow things down, you just don't notice because cable is built to share that one stream.

When everyone watches the Super Bowl on normal cable, the provider sends one copy of the broadcast to the neighborhood, and your box just tunes in to it. A million viewers use almost the same bandwidth as ten, because it's one shared signal, not a million separate copies.

During a crazy event - everyone refreshing a website, an app update dropping, a game launching - it's not one shared stream. Each person pulls their own copy from a server on the other side of the country. That's 50,000 separate transfers all hammering the same pipes, so everything feels like molasses.

You actually do see the cable version of this: when that huge shared stream gets reconfigured, your screen freezes on "no signal" for a few seconds. Same problem, just way more efficient.

So it's not that the Super Bowl doesn't affect the network - it totally does - it's that millions of people sharing one copy of a video is a lot lighter than millions of people each grabbing their own copy of a web page.

- Alex

Question: Why do need to be taught to lift with our legs and not our back? Is lifting with our back a learned behaviour that we need to unlearn?
original:
Hey Sam,

Great question, and one I've actually thought about more than I expected.

Short answer: yes, lifting with your back is a learned behaviour, mostly learned from not being told anything else. When we're little we pick up toys, dogs, bags of chips - small stuff, and bending at the waist is the path of least resistance. Nobody sits you down and says "hinge at your hips, push the floor away". We just watch Mum bend to pick up the laundry and we copy the whole motion, back and all. So it's less that we learn a bad technique than that we never learn the good one. The bending-at-the-waist version is what happens by default, so it fills in the gap.

The leg version has to be taught because it's counterintuitive. It feels weird to sit your hips back like you're reaching for a chair that isn't there, keep your chest up, and *then* stand. Your first few times, it looks ridiculous and feels like it takes more effort, because you're consciously driving a movement your body has on autopilot the other way. That's the unlearning part - you have to override a habit, not just add a new skill.

Also worth saying: a flat back and bent knees isn't automatically "lifting with your legs" either. The actual trick is keeping your spine in a neutral curve and letting your hips do the work, with the legs doing the pushing. People get told "lift with your legs" and interpret that as "bend your knees", which helps some but isn't the whole thing. The back stays straight either way - the difference is whether your hips move or your spine rounds.

So yeah, unlearn the rounding, learn the hinge, and it clicks after a while.

Talk soon,
Alex

Question: A few questions on house-buying stuff
original:
Hi Sam,

Thanks for the email - happy to help with the house stuff. A few thoughts:

First, get pre-approved for a mortgage before you start looking. It tells you your real budget and makes sellers take you seriously. Ask a couple of different lenders for rates, they vary more than you'd think.

Second, budget for the extras beyond the price: stamp duty, solicitor, surveys, moving costs. Easily another 5-10% on top, so don't max out your loan on the purchase price alone.

Third, get a proper building survey done, not just the lender's valuation. It'll pick up problems (damp, roof, wiring) that you can then use to negotiate the price down or just walk away.

And don't fall in love with the first house you see - look at a proper run of them so you can compare and not overpay for one you've got attached to.

Send me the specifics (location, price range, how much cash down) and I can be more useful. Have you got a solicitor lined up yet?

Cheers
Alex

Question: What does the little ball inside a whistle do?
original:
Hi Sam,

Oh nice, you finally noticed the little ball. So what you've got is a "fipple whistle" design (which is basically what all shop-bought whistles are), and that little ball is what actually makes it make a proper whistle sound in the first place.

Here's the deal: when you blow into a bare whistle with nothing inside, air just whooshes across the fipple and you get a soft, thin hiss that goes up in pitch the harder you blow. Not very whistle-like at all. But that little ball (called a "sounding ball" or "clicker") is a loose metal ball sitting in a shallow little depression in the middle of the cap, and it's held in by the cap so it can't fall out. When you blow, the air hits the ball and it bounces around in there, and each tiny bounce chops the airflow into a bunch of little pulses. Those pulses are what create the loud, reedy, fixed-pitch "peep" sound instead of a hiss.

The important part is the pitch doesn't really change with how hard you blow. The harder you go, the faster the ball rattles around and the louder it gets, but the pitch stays the same, because the pitch is actually set by the size of the air chamber in the body, not by the ball. The ball's only job is to chop the airflow up.

Which is also why a whistle that's jammed up with gunk or a bit of rust under the ball sounds like a dying souffle instead of a proper peep, and why you can sometimes fix an old one by taking the cap off and shaking the ball free.

Hope that clears it up! Happy to lend you mine to take apart if you want to confirm.

Cheers,
Alex

Question: Why are archers in movies instructed to fire all at once?
original:
Hi Sam,

Fun question, and honestly one I've wondered about too. The short version: it's about safety, and it's a real rule on set, not just a movie convention.

When you shoot archery in a film, the arrows are usually wooden practice points, and the "targets" are often dummies, shields, or props that people are standing right behind or near. If everyone fired on their own timing, you'd have arrows in the air at all heights and angles for the whole scene, and someone standing behind a dummy could get hit by an arrow that was meant for something else.

So the armorer, who's the person responsible for all weapon and arrow safety on a movie set, calls "loose!" and everyone lets go at literally the same instant. That way all the arrows are travelling in the same direction at the same time, along one planned line of flight. The armorer has cleared that line in advance: everyone who wasn't supposed to be in it has moved, the dummies are in position, and spotters are watching the landing area. One release, one beam of arrows going where they're supposed to go, everyone accounted for, and then a "reset" before the next take.

It's basically the same logic as the "guns for effect" rule in a Western with real firearms. You don't want shots going off on individual timing with people milling around; you want one coordinated moment so the whole area has been cleared for that specific instant.

And a small bonus: it looks a hell of a lot cooler on screen, and it re-inforces the safety thing, since everyone is definitely paying attention to the call if they release together. A wall of arrows all releasing together, all thwacking into the targets in the same frame, that's a great shot. A dozen guys twisting and releasing at random over ten seconds looks messy and you can't edit it into anything. So the safety rule and the "it looks better" rule conveniently point the same direction, so nobody on set argues with it.

Anyway, that's my best answer from memory. Let me know if you want me to track down an actual film armorer talking about it, I'm pretty sure there's an interview floating around where someone explains exactly this.

Talk soon,
Alex

Question: Why does my nose get runny when I eat/drink something hot.
original:
Hey Sam,

Ha, I had this exact same thing for years and was convinced I was just cursed with a leaky nose. Turns out it's actually pretty common - it even has a name, "gustatory rhinitis", which just means runny nose triggered by eating.

The short version is that the nerves in your nose are basically overreacting to the heat. When you eat or drink something hot, the warmth hits the back of your throat and the lining of your nose, and there are nerve endings there that can't really tell the difference between "hot soup" and "irritant in the airway". So your brain goes "oh no, something's irritating the nose" and does the one thing it knows how to do, which is flood the place with watery mucus to wash it out. Hence the snot within like ten seconds of your first sip of tea.

A few things that make it worse:

Spicy food is the big one. Capsaicin in chillies also activates the same nerves, and it does it way harder than plain heat does, which is why a spicy ramen bowl is basically a personal weather event. If yours is mostly triggered by spice rather than just temperature, that's classic.

It's usually the vapor, not the liquid itself. Hot drinks do it more than hot food I think, because the steam hits your nose directly. Same reason it's worse in a steamy kitchen.

And if you've ever had a cold or some nasal inflammation recently, it makes the whole thing worse for a while, because the nerves are already sensitised.

There's not really a proper cure, it's more a thing you just live with, but a few things help. Eating a little slower and letting food cool down a touch makes a real difference. Some people swear by an antihistamine before a big meal, though honestly that only works for some people and not others. The one thing that actually works for a lot of people is an ipratropium nasal spray, which is a prescription thing in some places that specifically dries up exactly this kind of runny nose without making you drowsy like the other sprays. Worth asking your doc about it if it's really getting to you.

Otherwise yeah, just keep a napkin in your pocket and live your life.

Anyway let me know if you want the doc's name for the spray, I used to know a guy who worked at the pharmacy.

Cheers
Alex

Question: How can scientists create measuring tools more accurate than the tools we already have? Doesn't the accuracy of new tools depend on the accuracy of the tools used to make it?
original:
Hi Sam,

Fun question. Yes, new tools do depend on the old ones, but you can still push past them because you rarely need one perfect tool. A few tricks: measure the same thing several different ways and average out each method's error; use feedback and compare the new device against the old one while calibrating on the fly; and lean on physical standards that don't need a better tool to define them, like the fixed time it takes light to travel a set distance or an atom's natural vibration frequency. Once you lock to that natural constant, your ruler or clock is tied to something universal, not to whatever device built it. Each generation borrows strengths from several older tools at once, so accuracy climbs step by step instead of being capped by any single one.

Best,
Alex

Question: Why do humans get time suppression during tragic events?
original:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and I love that you named it that way. The effect is real, though "time suppression" is the lay term, so let me riff on what's actually happening.

During trauma or shock, the amygdala takes over and the prefrontal cortex basically goes half-offline. That means the parts of your brain that normally timestamp experiences, build a coherent timeline, and file memories into "then this, then that" are underpowered right when you need them most. So you get a memory that's vivid but temporally loose: fragments, no clear before/after, gaps you can't walk through, a sense that a whole day compressed into a minute or a minute stretched out. Stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) also mess with the hippocampus, which is where sequencing lives, so the "when did this part happen" tag essentially doesn't get written.

It's also partly attention: under threat your focus narrows to the salient stuff, so peripheral context that would normally anchor time just never gets recorded.

Net effect: the event feels both closer and farther than it should, and the timeline around it is mushy for a while.

Hope that helps,
Alex

Question: Why does my nose get runny when I eat/drink something hot.
original:
Hi Sam,

Haha, yeah, the runny nose thing. So it's actually really common and it's got a name - it's called a vasomotor or reflex response, and it's basically your nose overreacting to the heat.

Here's what's happening. The lining of your nose is packed with tiny blood vessels and mucus glands. When hot food or soup or a hot drink comes up through your sinuses and nasal passages, the heat irritates that lining. Your nose responds the way it responds to pretty much any irritation - it cranks up mucus production and the blood vessels swell - because mucus is basically how your nose deals with things it doesn't like. So the heat gets read as "something's bothering me" and your nose floods.

There's a nerve component too. There are nerve endings in your nasal passages that connect to the part of your nervous system that controls things like mucus secretion (the parasympathetic side). Hot and spicy food can trigger those nerves to basically tell your mucus glands "produce more" without there being any actual intruder. So it's a bit of a false alarm - the heat sets off the reflex and your nose just goes.

Spicy food makes it a lot worse for the same reason - capsaicin in chillies hits those same nerve receptors even harder, which is why a hot curry will absolutely drench you. Some people are just more sensitive to this than others; it's a bit genetic how strongly your reflex fires.

It's not an allergy or anything to worry about unless it's coming with other stuff like sneezing fits, itchy eyes, or actual swelling, in which case it might be something else worth a look. But the plain "hot soup = runny nose" version is just a normal overzealous reflex and totally fine. You're not alone in it either - most people have it to some degree, it's just that some folks' noses go from dry to absolutely wicking within two sips of tea.

The only real fixes are: let the food cool down a bit, eat it a little slower, or just keep a towel handy. Some people find a decongestant nasal spray before a big hot meal helps a little, but honestly the towel is usually the answer.

Anyway, hope that helps (and that your soup keeps your nose to itself a bit more).

Cheers,
Alex

Question: Why do some games have huge modding communities (Minecraft, Skyrim), whereas others have none at all?
original:
Hey Sam,

Great question, I've been thinking about this a lot lately. I think it comes down to a few things, most of which the developers decide before launch.

First, the engine and "lego" factor. Skyrim and Minecraft are basically sandboxes with a ton of exposed pieces. Question: Why do giant pandas seem to have such terrible motor skills?
original:
Hi Sam,

Great question, and I had the same thought the first time I saw a video of a panda flopping backwards trying to drink some water.

The short answer is: they're not actually clumsy, they're just built wrong for being agile. Their whole body plan gets reused for one trick - gripping bamboo - which makes everything else look terrible. Pandas have a modified wrist bone (the "false thumb", actually an enlarged sesamoid bone in the wrist) that they use to grip stalks like primates do. But that same adaptation makes their forepaws stiff and awkward for anything else, like holding onto a tree.

On top of that they're basically round. Big belly, short legs, not much neck. Their center of gravity is high and stable for waddling, but it means one slip and the whole thing goes over. And they're deliberately slow - they eat 12-38 hours a day of low-calorie bamboo, so there's no selection pressure to be quick and coordinated. Evolution basically decided "good enough not to die" and stopped.

So it's less bad motor skills and more a body optimized for one narrow job doing everything else badly.

- Alex

Question: If Muhammad was "just" a prophet, then why do Muslims treat his persona at a level above what modern Christians treat Jesus Christ?
original:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and one I've actually thought about a lot.

Short answer: it's less about the person and more about what the religion asks of that person's traces. In Islam Muhammad isn't just a prophet in the way Christian "prophet" covers Jeremiah or Amos, he's the final one, "the seal of the prophets." That finality is partly theological but it also makes him legally and practically central: the Quran was revealed in and through him, the hadith and his practice (the sunna) form the second pillar of law after the Quran, and piety is explicitly defined as following his example. So his persona sits inside the daily practice at every level, not just the devotional one.

Modern Christianity also has a long tradition of separating the savior from the daily: Jesus is worshipped and obeyed through doctrine and sacrament, not by imitating his habits of dress, food, or courtship. No one's sinning for eating shrimp. Muslims are expected to pattern even mundane life on his practice. So the gap you're noticing is real, but it's the difference between a god you pray to and a law-giver you imitate.

Also, huge variation within both religions, obviously. Lots of everyday Muslims don't orbit his persona anywhere near as much as the question implies.

Anyway, that's my take. Ping me if you want book recs.

Best,
Alex

Question: Why do some games have huge modding communities (Minecraft, Skyrim), whereas others have none at all?
original:
Hey Sam,

Great question, I've been wondering this myself. I think it comes down to a few things that mostly have to do with how the game was built and how the developers treat outsiders.

First, the format of the game files. Skyrim runs on the Creation Engine, which stores everything in plain-ish, well-documented file formats ( textures, meshes, dialogue, whole quests). Someone with a hex editor and some patience can peek inside a game file on day one and figure out things. Minecraft is JSON and simple block data. Compare that to a game where everything is packed into one opaque proprietary blob with no documentation - modders give up after an afternoon. You need readable files, ideally with a published file format reference.

Second, how the game's logic works. If the core gameplay rules are hard-coded in compiled C++, mods can only change the surface stuff: models, textures, new character names. If the rules are written in a scripting language (Skyrim's Papyrus, Minecraft's Java, or better yet, source-available like CS:Goldsrc or Half-Life), modders can change how things *work*, add new mechanics, build whole new mode on top. That's the difference between "reskin" mods and "actually different game" mods. People stick around for the latter.

Third, the developer's stance. Half-Life 2, Skyrim, Minecraft, Factorio - the devs published tools or at least didn't sue you and said "yeah go ahead." Day of Defeat and CS communities blew up because Valve explicitly supported it. On the other side, some games ship with DRM that breaks if you touch a file, or EULAs that say modding is illegal, and the community just never forms. A "don't be weird" attitude is enough to kill it.

Fourth, accidentally: multiplayer. For whatever reason, single-player games get modded way more because modding a multiplayer game means you need everyone playing the same version, which is a coordination nightmare. Skyrim works; a modded version of an online game doesn't, unless the game has a dedicated modload-sharing system.

And there's a bit of a flywheel - once a modding community exists, they build the load tools, the tutorials, the forums, and that lowers the barrier so more people join, which means more tools. Games that miss the early wave at launch basically never catch up.

So in short: readable files, moddable logic, dev permission, and single-player. Get all four and you get Skyrim. Miss any one and you get a game where "modding" means swapping the main menu music.

Let me know if you actually want to mod something, I might take a look at your idea.

- Alex

Question: How do G force suits work?
original:
Hey Sam,

Ha, good one. Been meaning to figure this out properly myself.

So the basic problem is: at high g, your blood gets slammed toward your feet and pelvis by inertia. Your heart just can't pump hard enough to push it back up to your brain, so you get grey-out and then blackout, usually around 4-5 g sustained. The suit is basically a countermeasure for that.

It's a whole lot simpler than it looks, really. There's a network of bladders, little fabric chambers, running across your legs, belly, and thighs. Normally they're deflated and flat against the suit, so you don't notice them. But when the g's come up, compressed air (or sometimes nitrogen) gets pumped into them and they inflate. When they inflate they wrap around your lower body and press in, kind of like a really aggressive vend seal pipeline on your legs and gut, except the pressure is controlled and it's on the outside.

The trick is the pressure is measured against the g-load, so the tighter it squeezes as you pull harder, the more it squeezes. This does two things. One, it keeps the blood from pooling down in your legs by physically compressing the veins so the blood can't just sit there. Two, it compresses the abdominal vessels too, which helps your heart actually move blood uphill instead of just having it all slide down.

The whole thing is pretty fast - the air pumps kick in within a fraction of a second of the g's building, which is about the only way you'd survive a tight pull. Without the suit at 6 or 7 g you'd lose consciousness in like two seconds, and if you black out mid-maneuver you usually crash.

You can actually feel it. Pilots describe it as the suit going "on" - your legs get tight, your belly gets squeezed, it's a little uncomfortable but way better than the darkness. There's a control where you can adjust how hard it squeezes, which is annoying to figure out on the first few flights because you either feel like someone's in a vice or you don't feel enough of it.

Also the anti-g straining maneuver - where you tense your whole lower body on command - works with the suit, not instead of it. You still have to do the maneuver, the suit just extends how long you can hold it before going dark.

Anyway that's the short version. Want me to dig up some actual pilot accounts for you?

Cheers,
Alex

Question: The difference between a parody and a satire
original:
Hey,

Good question, and people mix the two up a lot. Short version: satire aims at something in the real world - a politician, an industry, a social habit - and wants you to see the problem with it. Parody aims at a specific work or style - a movie, a song, a genre - and copies it to make it look silly.

So satire targets ideas, parody targets form. Satire can stand on its own, but parody only lands if you recognize what it is imitating; the joke falls apart if you have not seen the original. They overlap a lot - a sketch of the nightly news is usually both parody of the news format and satire of the news itself - but the dividing line is that parody needs one specific original to mock, satire does not.

Anyway, hope that helps!

- Alex

Question: Why are archers in movies instructed to fire all at once?
original:
Hi Sam,

Funny question that I finally got a real answer to from a guy who does stunt
coordinator work on set. The "fire all at once" thing is not actually about
the arrows or the archers, it's about the camera and the sound. When two or
three archers loose at slightly different times, you get this scattered,
accidental-looking salvo, and on screen it just reads as sloppy and
uncoordinated. If everyone looses on the same beat instead, you get one clean
whoosh of arrows leaving the string and one clean thud when they land, and
that's way easier to sell to an audience than a dribble of individual
shots. So the director is really just trying to get a single synchronized
sound and a single synchronized moment of impact in the edit, and the only
reliable way to get that is to have everyone actually draw and release
together on his mark.

There's also the problem of the off-screen archers. The stunt coord counts
the group in or calls "draw" and "loose" as one group call, and if the
archers are scattered across the set at different distances and different
draw lengths, doing it on a counted rhythm gets messy fast because people
anticipate at different rates. One shouted "loose" cue is the simplest
thing that keeps the whole group landing on the same frame. And practically
speaking, an arrow hitting someone's shield a half second before the person
next to him even looks up reads as an accident in the final cut, so the
stunts want everyone committed at the same instant.

The flip side, and this is the part archers actually complain about, is
that this is one of the least realistic things in most movies. Real volleys
are deliberately staggered a little, partly so the archer in the front row
isn't shooting into the back of the archer behind him, and partly so you
don't have forty arrows in the same patch of sky at once, which would be a
genuine hazard to your own side. So the movie rule is basically: sacrifice
the realism, keep the sound effect clean, and give the editor one good
cut point to work with instead of four messy ones.

Anyway, that's my best version of it. Let me know what clip started this,
I'd like to see it.

Talk soon,
Alex

Question: Why does cheese taste so much better when it's melted?
original:
Hi Sam,

Great question, and honestly one of my favorite things to think about. Melted cheese tastes better for a few stacked reasons, and none of them are just in your head. The whole effect is temperature, texture, and chemistry all lining up at the same time.

First, temperature does a lot of the work on its own. Cold food mutes flavor, period. Cheese straight out of the fridge is somewhere around 4C, and your taste buds are far less responsive at that temperature. Warm food releases way more of its volatile aroma compounds, and since a huge chunk of what we experience as taste is actually smell traveling up the back of your nose, a warm slice or a melted slice hits you with so much more aroma than a cold one. So even before any of the chemistry kicks in, just warming the cheese up makes it smell more like itself.

Then the actual melting changes the matrix. Cheese is a structure of proteins and fat, and when it is solid a lot of those flavor molecules are locked inside it. As it heats, the protein network loosens up and the fat separates out and spreads. Fat is doing double duty here: a lot of the flavor compounds in cheese are fat-soluble, so the fat is literally carrying the flavor around, and it coats your tongue and the inside of your mouth, which makes the whole thing taste richer, rounder, and smoother. A cold solid wedge gives you flavor in small bites; melted cheese delivers it as a continuous film across your tongue, which your brain reads as more flavor even though it is technically the same cheese.

And for a lot of cheeses, especially the melty ones, heating and then browning a little on a pizza or a griddle adds a Maillard set of notes. Those toasty, nutty, caramelized bits do not exist in the cold cheese at all. That is the part you can never replicate with a cold slice, and I would argue it is the part people get most excited about.

So the short version: warmer means more aroma released, melted means the fat is spread out coating your whole mouth with flavor, and toasted means there are brand new browned flavor compounds in there that were not there when it was cold. All three stacked on top of each other at once.

Anyway, happy to defend whether a grilled cheese beats a pizza crust on this, because I have strong feelings. Let me know when you are free for a cheese debate over lunch.

Alex

Question: How do G force suits work?
original:
Hi Sam,

Funny you should ask, I was just reading about that. So a G-suit, or more formally an anti-g suit, is basically just a lot of fabric inflatable bladders strapped around your thighs and belly. The idea is that when a pilot pulls hard into a turn, all their blood wants to rush down toward their feet, and if enough of it does, the brain runs short of blood and they gray out and pass out. At maybe 5 or 6 Gs that starts happening to an unaided pilot, and fighter jets can easily push 8 or 9.

The suit works by sensing the G load the pilot is in. When it gets above a certain point, air is pumped into the bladders and they tighten up, squeezing the legs and lower abdomen. That compression does two things: it stops blood from pooling down in the legs by basically acting like a really aggressive pair of compression stockings, and it pushes some of the blood back up toward the upper body so the brain keeps getting its supply. When the Gs drop off, the air vents back out and the suit relaxes.

The weird thing about them is they're really only effective on the lower half of the body. Blood in the arms and head doesn't really benefit, which is why pilots tear into the whole thing by straining and tensing their whole body, kind of a forced breath-hold-manual-pump thing, and they're trained to do it in a specific breathing pattern. The suit handles the legs, the pilot handles the rest. Modern ones also use the pilot's seat placed slightly head-down-ish to help, but that's the aircraft not the suit.

Older versions used water or something, but modern ones are all air-operated and pretty light. They really only matter above about 3.5 or 4 Gs sustained, and they make a noticeable difference between maybe 6 and 9 Gs, which is about the range that's dangerous.

Anyway I hope that clears it up, let me know if you want me to dig up the actual engineering details.

Cheers
Alex

Question: Why do need to be taught to lift with our legs and not our back? Is lifting with our back a learned behaviour that we need to unlearn?
original:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and the short answer is: no, bending your back to pick things up isn't really a learned behaviour we need to unlearn, but it does feel natural, which is why it's worth coaching.

Babies and toddlers do actually squat or half-kneel a lot when they grab things off the floor, so the movement pattern itself is instinctive. What happens as we grow up is that we stop doing it. Squatting to lift is more effort, a bit undignified, and takes more space, so we gradually drift into a "hips back, round the back, arms do the work" stance because it's the path of least resistance. We pick that up by imitation and habit - watching how adults bend over, and getting away with it because most things we carry are light enough that nothing breaks. So it's learned in the loose sense of habit, but it's not some ingrained motor programme you're fighting against.

The reason the advice sticks to "lift with your legs" is about the spine. A rounded lower back under load puts the force onto the discs as compression plus bending, which is the combination that injures them. If you keep the back relatively straight and bend the hips and knees, the load sits mostly in compression along the spine, which it's very good at handling - and the big leg and glute muscles take the hard work, which is what they're built for. Legs can generate way more force than your back muscles can absorb, so using them is also just the strong option.

It's easier to pick the habit up than you'd think. Once you consciously set your hips back and stand up out of the knees a few times, it starts to feel about as natural as the bent version.

Anyway, hope that makes sense. Let me know if you want to go to the gym and I'll supervise your form.

Cheers,
Alex

Question: Where does all the rock salt for keeping the roads clear go? Why haven't so many areas near roads become too salty for grass, trees etc. ?
original:
Hi Sam,

Good question! Most of the rock salt doesn't pile up by the roadside - it dissolves into the snow and mucks up into storm drains, so it flows off with the rainwater into ditches, streams, and rivers, getting spread and diluted over a huge area. That's why local soil salt levels stay modest instead of building up year after year; the runoff keeps moving it away. You do see damage where it concentrates - pot-holes in fences, leaning street trees, patches of dead grass right at the road edge - but the salt that ends up in waterways is diluted enough that the immediate surroundings mostly recover.

Best,
Alex

Question: Why when a crazy event the isps slowdown but when millions watch the superbowl the cable stream isn't effected?
original:
Hey Sam,

Good question! There are really two separate things going on here.

First, when "crazy event" traffic spikes - like everyone in town suddenly downloading a game update, a big leak drops, or a local site goes viral - that traffic is all different destinations. It floods the same limited pipes your ISP uses to reach the rest of the internet, and since it's all new, scattered traffic, the network gets congested and everything slows down. ISPs also sometimes purposely throttle or deprioritize certain traffic when the network gets loaded, so you feel it.

The Superbowl is different because cable streams use totally different equipment. Your cable box gets the show from the ISP's own headend - basically a TV signal sitting inside their local network, not something being pulled from a streaming server on the open internet. It's like received over your local antenna, just over coax instead of air. So even if the internet path is jammed, the TV signal takes a shortcut that never touches the busy part.

Also, ISPs plan for the Superbowl specifically. They know millions of people will watch, so the stream is cached and distributed inside their network ahead of time - not a surprise load at all.

So: cable = internal shortcut + pre-planned, crazy events = all your traffic jammed onto the same external road.

- Alex

Question: What does the little ball inside a whistle do?
original:
Hi Sam,

Ha, good question — I kept wondering about that too and never actually thought it through. So I looked one up properly. That little ball (it's a small metal or plastic ball, called a "trill ball" or "pea") is the whole reason a pea whistle goes "pea pea pea" instead of just a plain blow.

Here's what happens: when you blow through the whistle, the air stream hits the ball and flicks it around inside the chamber. The ball keeps bouncing back and forth, and each time it blocks the air hole and then moves aside again, it chops the airflow into little bursts. That rapid on-off-on-off is the trilling sound you hear. Without the ball sitting there rattling around it's just a steady tone, like a slide whistle or a simple pea-less whistle.

The size and weight of the ball matter too — a bigger or lighter ball rattles around faster, so it trills at a higher rate, while a heavier one trills slower. That's why pea whistles sound a bit different from each other even when they're the same size and pitched to the same note.

Fun fact: referee whistles work the same way, which is why they sound so annoying when you try to blow one gently — the ball just doesn't get going properly and you get this wobbly half-trill instead of a proper blast.

Let me know if that made sense or if you want me to explain it like you're five. I owe you a drink for making me think about this at work today.

Cheers,
Alex

Question: Why do some games have huge modding communities (Minecraft, Skyrim), whereas others have none at all?
original:
Hey Sam,

Great question, this one actually comes up a lot. I think it's a mix of a few things.

First, the game itself has to be built in a way that's easy to poke at. Minecraft and Skyrim are basically data files and relatively simple rule systems. Skyrim's mods are mostly new meshes, textures, and scripts in a scripting language the developers actually documented and gave tools for (Creation Kit). Minecraft's world is just blocks, so you can add new blocks or dimensions without understanding the whole engine. Compare that to a modern AAA shooter where everything is compiled, obfuscated, and locked in proprietary containers. There's literally nothing to open. So the biggest factor is: did the developers make the game's content readable and editable, and did they ship tools?

Second, the game needs to be open-ended enough that adding stuff makes sense. In Skyrim you can add a quest, a dungeon, a weapon, a race - the game's structure has slots for all of that. In a linear story game, adding a new level doesn't fit anywhere, and adding new dialogue breaks the script. Games with big "content budget" categories (items, quests, maps, characters) mod way better than games where the fun is a fixed sequence of experiences.

Third, distribution and updates. Steam Workshop took a lot of the friction out of "how do I share this mod and how do I keep it working when the game updates." Skyrim launching basically next to Workshop made a huge difference. Without an easy way to share and update mods, communities die young because every mod is a broken zip file on some random forum.

Fourth, timing and culture, which is messy. Some games with modding-friendly tech never got communities because nobody in the modding scene liked the genre at the time. And some got crushed when the developer shipped updates that broke everything and never fixed it - that kills a community faster than anything else.

There's also the more cynical version: some publishers deliberately lock games down because mods can cannibalize DLC sales or complicate anti-cheat, and some just don't care because they're making a sequel in two years anyway.

So short version: open file formats + official tools + open-ended structure + easy distribution + devs who don't break or abandon the mods. Get most of those right and the community basically builds itself.

Anyway, I could go on forever. Want me to point you at some good video essays on this?

- Alex

Cheers,
Alex

Question: With so many ways to listen to an artists music for cheap or even free, how do musicians make any money?
original:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and it's a real puzzle. Streaming pays tiny fractions of a cent per play, so royalties from Spotify and the like barely cover anything unless you're getting millions of streams. Where the money actually comes from now: touring and live shows are the big one, merch sales at those shows, plus sync licenses when songs end up in films, shows, ads, and games. Question: Why do some games have huge modding communities (Minecraft, Skyrim), whereas others have none at all?
original:
Hey Jonas,

Great question - I've been thinking about it a lot lately since I've been deep in the Skyrim modding scene again.

I think it mostly comes down to a few things. First is whether the developers actually made it possible to tinker. Minecraft and Skyrim basically shipped with the door unlocked - Minecraft's files are plain and you can start making texture packs just by renaming .png files; Skyrim got full creation tools released to everyone from day one, so adding quests and items feels approachable. Compare that to a AAA FPS where everything is packed, encrypted, or locked behind a network layer - there's literally nothing a tinkerer can open on their machine. No tools, no readable data, no entry point, and the community can't even start.

Second is the shape of the game. Single-player world games are modding goldmines because a mod is just "me + the game" - no compatibility problems, no balance concerns, you break whatever you want and only your playthrough breaks. Online multiplayer is much harder because any change has to work for hundreds of people at once and servers have to verify things to prevent cheating, so you end up with either a very restrictive API or none.

Third is scope. Modding thrives when the game defines a world and leaves big empty spaces in it. Minecraft gives you a kit of blocks and says "world?" Then there's the ecosystem that kicks in once you have a few hundred mods: Steam Workshop, Nexus, tutorials, forum help. It's self-reinforcing - the big scene attracts more modders, which makes more content. Miss the critical mass early and the scene quietly dies, even if the game was technically moddable.

So it's usually a stack: devs left it open + the game had room for additions + the community crossed the critical mass. Miss one and you're looking at an empty Nexus page.

original:
Привет, Саня!

Рад, что письмо дошло, и спасибо за вопрос, он кстати неплохой, я сам часто задумываюсь об этом. Пытаюсь коротко расписать, только без учебника, чтобы не уснуть, и без всяких графиков, их в тексте всё равно нормальных не нарисовать. Так что будет по пунктам, как я понял, и если что перепутаю, поправь.

Во-первых, денежная политика, это когда центробанк рулит процентной ставкой. Ставка высокая, кредиты дорогие, все меньше берут, меньше тратят, инфляция остывает, но и экономика как бы притормаживает. Ставка низкая, кредиты дешёвые, все за деньги борются, экономика разгоняется, но и цены ползут вверх. Так что это как газ и тормоз одновременно. Ещё центробанк может печатать деньги или выкупать облигации — это уже жёстче, но тогда всегда риск, что денег станет слишком много и всё просто подорожает.

Во-вторых, фискальная политика, то есть бюджет: налоги и расходы. Государство может поднять налоги, тогда у всех меньше денег на расходы, или наоборот снизить, и люди побольше тратят. А может само потратить побольше — строить дороги, школы, больницы, это прямо вливает деньги в оборот, рабочие места появляются, подрядчики зарабатывают. Только если тратить постоянно в долг, получается долг на всех нас в будущем, потом нашим детям придётся отдавать.

В-третьих, регулирование. Можно вводить лицензии, антимонопольные правила, всякие требования к бизнесу. Строгие правила — больше бюрократии, бизнесу тяжелее, но и от обмана потребителей защита. Мягкие — бизнесу легче, но и обмануть проще. Тут баланса искать.

В-четвёртых, прямое участие: госкомпании в стратегических отраслях, дотации тем, кого считают важным развивать, например зелёную энергетику сейчас всем нравится дотировать. Работает, когда рынок сам туда не пойдёт, но может и частный капитал вышибать.

В-пятых, внешняя торговля: тарифы на импорт, квоты, субсидии тем, кто на экспорт. Защищает своих производителей, но соседи отвечают тем же, и нам самим дешевле ничего не становится, потому что импорт дороже.

В общем, все эти рычаги так или иначе влияют на спрос, на цены и на то, куда в итоге идут деньги. И ни один не идеален, потому что любое вмешательство где-то что-то ломает, вопрос только где и сколько. Помнишь, как дедушка говорил, что в экономических вопросах главное — влезай, а там всё равно где-то скрипнет? Вот примерно так. Если расскажешь, для чего спрашиваешь — курс, спор с папой? — тогда упрощу или усложню по ситуации.

Держись, напиши как там у тебя, и что там у вас на работе нового было, уже месяц молчишь.

Обнимаю,
Лёха

Спасибо за письмо, вопрос хороший. Обследование на ИППП обычно начинают с визита к урологу или венерологу — врач расспросит об отношениях, симптомах и осмотрит, а уже потом назначит анализы. Сдают в основном: кровь на сифилис и ВИЧ, мазок или ПЦР из уретры на хламидии, гонорею, микоплазму и уреаплазму, мазок из зева и соскоб с гениталий на герпес при необходимости, а также общий анализ мочи. Женщинам прибавляются мазки из шейки матки и влагалища. Сдавать лучше натощак за пару часов до анализа без мочеиспускания, и за день лучше не принимать антибиотики. Результат крови готов на второй-третий день, ПЦР чуть дольше.

Всё, вопросов больше не имею, напиши как приедешь.

Целую
